Would like recs for films heavily inspired by Douglas Sirk beyond Far From Heaven (and other Todd Haynes) and The Shape of Water.
Fassbinder like Ali: Fear Eats the Soul and The Bitter Tears of Petra von Kant etc., Almodovar like All About My Mother etc. most of his films are inspired by Sirk.

All of Fassbinder. Angst essen Seele auf and Petra von Kant would be the usual suspects but really, there's a bit of Sirk in all he made. My favourite far and away if Berlin Alexanderplatz. Especially the ending is quite Sirkian but also very Godard. Fassbinder also helped Sirk produce his last short films in Germany.

I would also say you can distantly find some Sirk in the Berliner Schule. Petzold's films always have a bit of debt to Sirk, especially Phoenix but I feel like the social determination that permeates Sirk's work can be found in almost all his films. "Etwas Besseres als den Tod" (2011) I would also highly recommend which is one of his most romantic films. Or Jerichow (2008) which is more Fuller than Sirk though I guess.

If you want something that plays it a bit more straight and grander in scale try Almodovar, especially Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown.

Also less inspired by Sirk but rather growing from the same soil is the incredibly overlooked Helmut Käutner who started making films alongside Sirk in 1930's nazi Germany. Many of his films can be situated somewhere inbetween Ophüls and Sirk. Especially highly recommended is Große Freiheit Nr. 7 (1944) but also Romanze in Moll (1943), Unter den Brücken (1946) or Schwarzer Kies (1961). 

Also while we're at it watch Ophüls of course if you haven't already. Letter from an Unknown Woman (1948) is easily the most Sirkian and also watch Willi Forst, Maskerade (1934) for example. Many of the strategies Sirk uses stem straight from Weimar cinema so if you fish a bit in that pond you will find a lot of similarities, especially in how they intelligently deal with social constellations.

Hou Hsiao-hsien - Millennium Mambo (2001) recently got a great remaster and it's one of his best.

Apichatpong Weerasethakul - Tropical Malady (2004) and Syndromes and a Century (2006) provide a good starting point. I'd call Syndromes his masterpiece.

Michelangelo Antonioni - His 60s and 70s films are some of the greatest works of cinema, especially the early 60s trilogy of films.

Federico Fellini -  La Dolce Vita (1960) should fit perfectly what you're looking for.

Kōhei Oguri - Sleeping Man (1996) is all transcendent beauty, no plot. One of my all-time favorites.
I’d think you’d enjoy the 80s French films Jean de Florette and Manon des Sources. Simple provincial countryside life that builds in destiny and beauty.

Hi, I'm just a curious person.

Is there any kind of reusable film technology in real life that can be erased and reused over and over? I'm sure there is, but don't know what it's called.

For a fictional setting, I imagine a 50 frames per second contraption that on the front end is used like a computer monitor, but under the hood, it uses a reusable film that can be erased to a pristine state and developed within a 20ms cycle. So it's like epaper in a way, because the image is persistent. Maybe initially erasing is a slow process, so to make a 30 fps monitor in the early days. we have a film reel that quickly draws the next frame onto that piece of film and then switches it out with the current one, which then goes into a queue to be erased. And by the time of the book, the technology has been improved.

You're welcome. You might want to look at the Indian Parallel cinema movement. Of course you are already familiar with Satyajit Ray, but there are also other greats from it like Ritwik Ghatak and Mrinal Sen.

Ritwik Ghatak only directed 8 films and I could recommend any of them, but The Cloud-Capped Star might be easiest to track down since it has a Criterion re-release. For Mrinal Sen his Calcutta Trilogy is a great starting point: Interview (1971), Calcutta 71 (1972) and Padatik (The Guerilla Fighter) (1973).
Thank you so much man! I'm excited to check these guys out and learn more about indian cinema besides bollywood mainstream
